about: The words of the chain kentish_revolt_796 (Data/encounters/chain_kentish_revolt_796_793.json; Design/content/chains/kentish_revolt_796.md): Kent's rising against Mercia under Eadberht Praen, 796 to 798, and the Wantsum ports caught in it. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the three news items the cards post; one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture and one 'art.chain_kentish_revolt_796.ending.<name>' line for each ending. People: the reeve Wighelm and Archbishop Aethelheard are the spine's cast; Osmund is the guest master of places/quentovic.json; Eadberht Praen is historical; Heahred, Osnoth, Wigheard, Ealdhun and Beornheah are ordinary invented people. Quoted: in s10.intention and news.waste the words 'made inroads upon the inhabitants of Kent as far as the marsh' and 'led him bound into Mercia' are from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, tr. J. Ingram, 1823 (annal 796 for 798). Everything said of Alcuin's letter of 797 and of Pope Leo's letter of 798 is our own plain rendering, not a quotation. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Two tallies
Two men sit at the toll bench where one used to sit, each with his own tally stick, and neither looks at the other. The old one you know. The young one wears a sword at a toll bench, which is new.
King Offa died three days before Lammas. I have had no word since from anyone who can tell me to stop, so I sit here, and I cut the notch as I always did.
Kent has a king of its own kin again. Eadberht. The toll of this water is his, as it was his fathers' before any Mercian saw the sea. Pay it here.
They call him Praen. Priest. He was one. I am told a man can put down a book and pick up a kingdom. I have not seen it written where.
The Mercian's archbishop has gone, and nobody drove him. A shepherd who runs before the wolf is seen has told you what he thinks of the flock.
You have nothing aboard. Then for once this bench has nothing to quarrel over. Sit. It is the first quiet hour I have had since the hay.
That is iron under your boards. Do not carry it past Canterbury's landing. The king's steward there pays better than anyone you will find up the Thames.
Pay on the old tally, as you always have
Pay on the new king's tally
Sell nothing today, and ask who is king in Kent
The old man cuts his notch and splits the stick. The young one watches your sail all the way down the channel. Nobody stops you. Somebody will remember.
The young man cuts a new stick, badly, and gives you half. He says the steward at Fordwic is buying spearheads at any price. The old man looks at the water.
You sell nothing, and so owe nobody. By evening you have it from both of them: Offa is dead, a priest is king in Kent, and the archbishop is gone.
What the benches look like
The wic-reeve has heard you came up from the Wantsum. He asks what you saw at the toll benches of Kent, listens, and then asks it again in other words.
You came by Sarre. Who sat at the bench? One man or two? And who sat at the bench at Sarre? I ask twice because the second answer is usually shorter.
The old king is dead and his son is king. The son is not well. I say this to you because the whole Strand says it already.
King Ecgfrith lasted a hundred and forty-one days. I counted. King Coenwulf is no kin of his to speak of, and has Kent to mend before anything else.
No iron goes into Kent from this beach. Corn I cannot stop. Spearheads I can, and I know the weight of a bundle through a sack.
I hear you paid your toll on the wrong stick. A Frisian cannot be blamed for paying the man with the sword. Once.
I need eyes that pass Sarre and Dofras without being looked at. A Frisian keel is nobody's business. Thirty pennies now, and half toll here while it lasts.
Agree to bring him word of Kent each time you pass
Tell him Kent is quiet and poor, which is half true
Say you are a Frisian and count casks, not kings
He counts thirty pennies into your hand, old king's coin, and tells his toll man to take half from you until midsummer. You have a second trade now. It weighs nothing and it is hard to stow.
He nods slowly. Quiet and poor is what he hoped to hear, and men believe what they hope. He asks it once more, and you say it the same way.
He asks again, and your second answer is longer than your first. He thanks you. He does not offer you the bench by his fire.
He almost smiles. Then count this, he says: no wine has come round by the Wantsum since Lammas, and the Strand is paying a third over for a cask from the Seine.
A new name on the penny
At the landing below Canterbury a moneyer lays a bright penny on your thwart. It carries a king's name you have not read on silver before. Behind him a steward waits with a list.
Read it. EADBEARHT REX. Same dies cutter, same hammer, same arm. Last year I struck for Offa. A moneyer is like a ferry: he serves whichever bank he is on.
Weigh it against one of the old king's heavy ones. Go on. A new king cannot afford a light penny. Only an old king can.
The king's hall wants spearheads. Six bundles, landed here before the leaves are down. I pay near twice what they cost you on the Rhine, in that coin.
The king lived among the Franks when Offa wanted him dead. King Charles fed him. A Frisian is King Charles's man. So we are nearly friends already, you and I.
If iron frightens you, bring wheat. A hall that feeds armed men eats like a minster in Lent, only all year.
I will say what he will not. If the Mercian comes back, the man who landed spears here will be named, and the reeve at Lundenwic keeps long tallies. Corn has no name on it.
Take the order: six bundles of spearheads, landed here
Take an order for corn instead: men eat under any king
Weigh the new penny, praise it, and take no order
The steward notches a stick for six bundles and gives you half. You are Kent's ironmonger until the leaves fall. The moneyer has already turned away.
Twelve sacks of wheat, at half over the price. The steward is not pleased, and not displeased. A man who feeds you is hard to hang.
The penny is full weight and well struck, and you say so. The moneyer is pleased. The steward folds his list. You owe nothing to anyone in Kent, yet.
To the people of Kent
The guest master of Saint-Josse comes down to the Canche with a folded letter under his scapular. It is from his abbot, and it is addressed not to a man but to a whole people.
Abbot Alcuin holds this house by the king's gift, to lodge the English on their way to Rome. Now he writes to the English who stayed at home. To the Kentish. All of them.

He tells them to call their archbishop home. He tells them hardly a man is left anywhere of the old stock of kings, and that a people which keeps changing lords ends with strangers. He is kinder than that. But that is it.
Their king sat at this table once. Odberht, we wrote him down as: a priest, an exile, on his way to Rome with a letter from King Charles. He ate little and asked a great deal about ships.
I am told you carry iron to Kent. Then carry this too. A boat should not bring a land only the things that cut.
I will be honest. There are Kentish boats off the Foreland stopping keels for letters. This one is written to them, not about them. Whether the man with the spear can read is another matter.
Take the letter to Canterbury's landing
Take it, and stay three days to have a copy read to you
Say your boat is searched on both shores already
He gives you the letter, ten pennies for the freight, and a blessing that takes longer than both. It goes inside your shirt, where a king's boat looks last.

For three evenings he reads it to you, a line in Latin and a line in English. You learn the Latin for flock, for shepherd and for folly. The letter goes inside your shirt, and now you know its weight.
He is not angry. He says the letter will find a boat; letters do. You sail without it, and Kent hears the abbot from some other mouth, or does not.
Eight oars off the Foreland
A boat with eight oars pulls out from under the white cliff and holds water across your bow. A man stands in her with a spear grounded on the bottom boards. She has twice your men.
Whose keel, from where, and what is under your shirt? I ask the last because it is always the shirt.
The Mercian's bishop writes to his friends in Kent, and his friends write back. The king wants to read both. That is all this is. Heave to.
A Frisian. You people carry anyone's word for a penny. I do not say it to shame you. I say it because it is why I am out here in the wet.
Heave to and show the letter: it is written to Kent, not to Mercia
Heave to, let him turn the hold over, and say nothing
Bear away for the Goodwin shoals, where eight oars will not follow
He turns it over, finds the word for Kent on the outside, and spells it with his finger. A letter to us, he says, and hands it back as if it might be owed toll.
He cannot read it and will not say so. You lie alongside half a day while a boy runs for a priest. The priest reads the outside, shrugs, and you are let go with the tide lost.
They turn over every sack and sound the bilge with a spear butt. Nobody looks inside a wet Frisian's shirt. It costs you the best of the ebb.
You put her over the tail of the sands with a hand's breadth under the keel. Eight oars stop where the water changes colour. Your men do not speak until the Foreland is astern.
The wind drops and eight oars do not. They take forty pennies for the trouble and break the seal. When they have had it read to them they give it back, looking foolish. It is a letter to Kent.
A letter to everybody
A priest and the king's steward both meet your boat at the landing. Each holds out a hand for the same letter, and each says it is written to him.
It is written to the people. Then let the people hear it. Sunday, at the church door, in English, by me. I have the voice for it, and nothing left to lose but the voice.
A letter to the people of Kent is a letter to their king. He will read it, and tell the people what was in it that concerns them.
The seal is broken. The watch has told me how. I do not hold it against you. I only note that you ran.
Christ Church has been lighter of its silver since the archbishop went. I do not say who carried it out. I say I stayed, and counted what was left.
If it is read aloud, not everyone will like the sound. The last man who said the archbishop's name at that door had a stone for it. I tell you so that you stand to one side.
Have it read at the church door on Sunday, before whoever comes
Give it to the steward, for his king's eyes first
Put it in the priest's hand and go out on the ebb
He reads it twice, Latin and then English. Nobody throws anything. Old men nod at the part about the stock of kings. By evening all Canterbury knows which boat brought it.

At the archbishop's name a stone comes over the heads and takes you on the shoulder. The priest reads on, louder. He finishes. All Canterbury knows which boat brought it, and that her skipper bleeds like anyone.
The steward gives you forty of the new pennies and carries the letter up the hill. What the people hear of it is one sentence, on a market day, and it is not the abbot's.
The priest takes it in both hands. He will read it to those he trusts, behind a shut door. You are out past the Stour mouth before the tide has turned.
In whose coin
The old reeve's bench at Dofras has a new man on it. The king's hall has stores lying on the shingle that must go round to the Stour, and yours is the only keel on the beach.
Forty sacks and nine barrels, from here to Canterbury's landing. One tide round the Foreland. My own boats are out watching for other people's letters.
I will pay in the king's new pennies, a third over the rate. Or in Offa's, if you are fond of the dead, and then it is the bare rate. Or in cloth. The looms here do not care who is king.
Hereberht sat on that bench eleven years. One morning he was not on it. Nobody saw him go, and everybody knows the road he took.
Take the new pennies if you like. But think where you mean to spend them. On the Strand a man was asked last month where he got one, and the asking took all day.
The steward at Canterbury has spoken of you. You are down on his stick already. One more notch will not make you more of a Kentish man than you are.
Do the work for the new pennies, a third over the rate
Do it for old King Offa's pennies, and fewer of them
Do it for cloth off the Dofras looms
Say the tide does not serve, and drink your ale
One tide round, and a hundred and sixty bright pennies with a priest's name on them. They are good silver. Whether they are good company is another matter.
One tide round, and a hundred of the dead king's pennies, worn and heavy. Nobody anywhere will ask you where you got those.
One tide round, and seven bolts of Dofras cloth, the long kind. The alewife says it was her sister's weaving, and that you chose like a man with a wife.
The tide serves well enough and he knows it. He finds a fishing boat by evening. The alewife fills your cup again without being asked.
The answer from Rome
The reeve sends for you to the king's hall in the wic. A tonsured man in a travelling cloak sits by the wall with a book chest at his feet, and lets the reeve do the talking.
The king wrote to the pope about Kent. The answer has come. A priest cannot be a king. The pope has put Eadberht out of the Church, and says the king may put him out of Kent.
The king also asked that my seat be moved here, to London, away from the Kentish. The pope says no. Canterbury it was and Canterbury it stays. I find I am glad, which surprises me.
So the king goes into Kent after the hay, with everything Mercia has. I tell you because by then it will not matter who knows.
An army eats. The corn will go by water, round to the Wantsum, and my boatmen know the Thames and nothing else. You know the swatchways at Sarre. A hundred and twenty pennies now. More on the day.

You had the abbot's letter read at my church door. They know your boat. Then carry one thing more. If he lays the kingdom down before the army marches, the Church takes him back as a penitent, and I will ask the king to spare the land.
You carried the abbot's letter to Kent. I am told few heard it. A letter read behind a door is a seed kept in a bag.
Six bundles of spearheads were landed below Canterbury. I have the count. I do not yet have the name, and I am in no hurry. Names keep.
You paid for your ale last night with a penny I had not seen before. I have it here. Good silver. An odd name on it.
Agree to bring the king's corn boats through the Wantsum when the army goes
Carry the archbishop's offer to Kent: lay the kingdom down, and live
Say little, sail on the ebb, and tell Kent what is coming
Hear it out, and promise nothing to anyone
A hundred and twenty pennies, counted twice. You are to be at Sarre when the smoke shows. The archbishop looks at you once, and then at his book chest.
The archbishop writes six lines, folds them small and seals them with his ring. The reeve says he has seen nothing. Four days to Sarre, and a man there who will know your sail.

You say yes to nothing and are out on the ebb. At the first Kentish beach you tell it plainly: after the hay, with everything. They thank you. It is not news they can use, except to bury their silver.
You hear it out and promise nothing. The reeve is not surprised. On the Strand they are already saying it: the king goes into Kent this summer.
A night at the crossing
After dark a man fetches you to the ferryman's hut above the strand. Inside, by one rushlight, sits a man with a king's ring on his hand and the mark of an old tonsure under his hair.
You will stand there. You will say what you were given to say, and nothing of your own. If he asks for your own, be short.
He writes a good hand, the archbishop. He always did. Penance, a cell, my eyes and my hands left on me. He puts it more gently. I was a priest. I can read between a bishop's lines.
The pope, I am told, sets me beside Julian, who left the faith and took the purple. I left a book and took what was my fathers'. But the pope has the pen.
I have crossed that water once already with nothing. King Charles gave me bread and a letter. It is a hard thing to go back to a table as a guest when you left it to be a king.
Lord, we have spears now, and the men to hold them. The Mercian has a boy's claim and a dead king's debts. Do not hear this boatman.
You, Frisian. You have seen both benches and both halls. If you were a king with one ship's worth of friends, what would you do? Say it short.
Say it plainly: the army comes after the hay, and your boat can be over the water by first light
Remind them whose corn and whose toll Kent has had from you, and put it as a friend
Lay the letter on the table and wait on the strand for the tide; the choosing is theirs
He is quiet a long time. Then he takes off the ring and gives it to the thegn. I will not have Kent burnt for my name, he says. He is aboard before the moon is down, in a plain cloak, facing aft.
The thegn's hand is on his sword before you have finished. The king lifts one finger and it stops. Go back to your boat, he says. I was a priest once. I will not be one twice.

You name the sacks and the tallies. The thegn cannot say you are the Mercian's man. The king laughs, once. Fed by a Frisian and buried by a Mercian: no. He takes off the ring. He is aboard before the moon is down.
They hear you out, because you have earned that. Then the king says a friend's counsel is still a boatman's counsel, and that he will stand. He thanks you. He means it.

You wait on the strand until the flood. Nobody comes down. At Dofras, three days on, they say the king rode west with four men and took ship from the Marsh. His ring was found on the altar at Canterbury.
You wait on the strand until the flood. Near dawn the thegn comes down alone and gives you the letter back, unanswered. The seal has been mended with a thumb.
As far as the marsh

This year the king of the Mercians made inroads upon the inhabitants of Kent as far as the marsh. Smoke stands along the down, and the beach is full of people who have never asked the price of a passage before.
I am Beornheah. I had six hides by the Marsh this morning. I have a wife, two children and nine of my people on this shingle, and you have the only keel that floats.
They took the king at the edge of the Marsh. Bound, on a cart, facing backward. I saw it from the reeds. I did not come out of the reeds. Write that down too, if you are writing.
Frisian. I have a cup with a foot to it and six bolts of cloth and no wish to carry them to Tamworth. Sixty pennies. You will not see that price again.
I will be fair. The cup came off an altar. The archbishop's people are a day behind us, asking after such things. What you do with that is yours.
You are the Frisian for the corn boats. They are lying off the north mouth afraid of the mud. The reeve said you would come. He said it twice.
You told us at midsummer. We buried the silver and stayed with the land. The silver is still buried. I could not tell you now under which ash heap.
You were at the crossing that night. He could have gone. I was one of those who told him to stand. I say it to you because there is no one else left to say it to.
Take as many off the beach as she will carry, and ask nothing
Take the thegn's household over the water for his silver
Buy what the spearman has in his sack
Bring the king's corn boats through the Wantsum, as you said you would
Fourteen people and a dog, the water a hand below the rail. You land them on the Frankish side at dusk. The thegn has nothing to give you and says so, in front of his children.
A hundred and fifty pennies, old coin and new, counted on the shingle while the smoke comes nearer. Thirteen people. The thegn does not haggle. You both remember that he did not.
A silver cup with a foot, and six bolts that smell of smoke. Sixty pennies. The thegn watches from the shingle and says nothing, and goes to find another boat.
You bring eleven corn boats through on one flood, sounding with an oar. The Mercian steward pays a hundred and sixty on the bank. From the water the burning looks like harvest fires.
One tally again
There is one man at the toll bench again, and one tally. Behind him the hall roofs are black rafters, and the first thing he asks any skipper is whether he carries corn.
Cuthred is king in Kent. The king's brother. He did not ask to be. I am his reeve, and I did not ask either. We have that in common, the king and I.
They led the other one bound into Mercia. What was done to him there I did not see, and I will not describe it at a toll bench. He will not sign his name again, nor read it.
The archbishop is home. He walked through his own gate between two rows of people who would not look up. He has ordered corn for them before candles for the church.
The reeve at Lundenwic sent your name ahead of you. He writes that you were useful and that I should say so in a way you can spend.
You carried Abbot Alcuin's letter. The archbishop has a copy of it by his bed. He says the boat that brought it should not pay to tie up under his city.
You carried his offer to Sarre, and it was refused. He does not count that as failing. He says a man who was offered his eyes and chose his crown has no quarrel with the messenger.
You have some of the priest's pennies. So has everyone. The moneyer takes them by weight and strikes them again. Silver does not remember whose face it wore.
Ask the king's writing: one keel of yours free of toll at Sarre, as the abbess's ships are
Take what the archbishop offers the man who carried his word to Sarre
Ask the archbishop's protection for the boat that carried the abbot's letter
Take a burnt toft by the Sarre landing for the asking, and the reeve's order for seed corn

A strip of parchment with the king's cross and four witnesses: one keel of your house passes Sarre without toll, and if she is wrecked or worn out, another in her place. And seven hundred pennies, for corn boats brought through.

The clerk counts out eleven hundred pennies from the archbishop's own chest. Your keel lies free at Fordwic, and your house is written down as under the archbishop's hand. He asks you to pray for a blind man in Mercia.
Six hundred pennies and a leaf with the archbishop's mark: this house's boats are his guests on any water where his name counts. The clerk reads it to you in Latin first, to be sure you follow.

The reeve paces out a burnt toft above the landing and says it is yours if you roof it. He gives you two hundred and fifty pennies on the nail for seed corn, and will pay double for every sack till spring.
What Kent owes
The thegn of the Marsh finds your boat before you have made fast. He has a sea chest, a boy of twelve, and a way of standing that says the chest is all of it.
Kent owes you. The king's steward is dead and his tally with him, so I will pay it. Somebody of Kent should, and I am what is left standing.
They put out his eyes and cut off his hands. A priest's hands. I think of the Mass he used to say. I find I cannot stop thinking of it.
You took my people off the shingle and asked nothing. I had nothing. I have a little now, and I know every creek from the Stour to the Marsh. Half of both is yours if you will have me.
You took a hundred and fifty pennies from me on that beach. It was a fair price. I say fair. I do not say more.
I saw you buy from the spearman. I have thought about it. A man must fill his hold. Still, I saw it.
One thing you should know. The reeve at Lundenwic has your name on the same stick as mine. He is a patient man. Go carefully on the Thames.
Swear fellowship with him: his chest and his knowledge of the coast in a second boat
Take his coaster, got out of the Stour before the burning, against all that is owed
Take the last of his wool and be shown the swatchways of the Wantsum

You swear it on the boat's stem, his hand over yours. Six hundred pennies from the chest go into the common purse. He will sail the second boat, and there is no water between the Stour and the Marsh he cannot take her through at night.

She lies in the Canche with weed on her: a broad Kentish coaster, built for the minster's corn. He gives you her, and two hundred and fifty pennies, and says Kent is quit with you. The boy unships her oars himself.

Thirty bolts, the last cloth of his folds, and a hundred pennies. Then three days in a skiff, at low water, while he shows you where the Wantsum keeps its sand. He names every bank. Some are named for men he knew.
Two tallies, side by side
The Strand smells of wet ash. The reeve has two tally sticks on the table in the king's hall: what you did for his king, and what you did for the other one.
This stick is what you did for the king. This one is what you did for Kent. They are much the same length. I laid them together to be sure.
Half the wic burned this year, and more people than I can count. I have a town to feed and roof, and no time to hang a man who knows where corn is.
And these. Pennies with a priest's name, that came up the river in your purse. I have melted the rest of them. I kept yours.
So. You may be useful to me again, or you may be honest with me for the first time. I pay for either. I pay more for the first.
If you give me names, Kent will know who gave them. Kent is beaten. It is not dead. Their grandsons will have boats.
Buy his silence with names: who in Kent ordered iron, and who paid
Buy the Kentish trader he took at Fordwic, at a tenth of her worth
Say a merchant sells to whoever stands on the beach, and wait
You give him four names. He breaks the second stick over his knee. Eight hundred pennies, and a man of his to keep your goods on the Strand. At Sarre, from now on, nobody will catch your rope.
Three hundred pennies for a sea-going trader with her mast still in her. He says it is the price of a ship nobody else dares buy. He keeps both sticks. She still has a Kentish name cut in her stem.
He looks at you for some time. Then he laughs, the first time you have heard it. Six hundred pennies of earnest for the wic's corn. Use the Wantsum as you learned it. And know I keep both sticks.
Roofs still on
The landing below Canterbury is as it was: thatch on the halls, corn in the ricks, one man at the toll bench. The archbishop has walked down from the city himself to see a Frisian boat come in.
I came home through standing corn. I had expected ash. The king rode in with his army behind him and found nobody to fight, and an army with nobody to fight wants its own harvest.
He is at Saint-Josse, I hear, shaven again, reading. Abbot Alcuin writes that he is a poor penitent and a good librarian. He has his eyes. I think of that more than I thought I would.
Cuthred is king in Kent, the king's brother. The Kentish do not love him. But a king who burnt nothing is easier to pay toll to. I have had no trouble at this bench. None.
There is a matter of six bundles of spearheads. The archbishop has asked me to lose the stick. I have lost it. I am telling you so that you know it was a thing that could be found.
No chronicle will write this year down for Kent, because nothing happened. I count that your doing. Ask me for something. Ask sensibly; I am a Mercian's bishop in a Kentish town.
Ask the archbishop's protection, and a keel free of toll at Fordwic
Ask ground by the Stour and a clerk of the church to keep your goods there
Ask only what the abbess's ships have at Sarre, and give a tenth of the gift to the poor of Kent

Twelve hundred pennies from the church's chest, a leaf with his mark that puts your house under his hand, and a second with the king's cross: one keel free at Fordwic for as long as she swims, and another after her.

Nine hundred pennies, and a strip of ground between the Stour and the road, forty paces by twelve. A clerk of Christ Church will keep the key and the tally. He counts in Latin and cheats in neither tongue.

Six hundred pennies, and sixty of them go back up the hill for the poor before you have closed your hand. He gives you the freedom of Sarre and his protection besides, and says he asked you to be sensible, not holy.

King Offa died three days before Lammas. In Kent a man of the old kin, Eadberht, who was a priest, has made himself king, and the archbishop has left Canterbury. At the toll benches two men sit where one sat.
The pope has answered the king of the Mercians: a priest cannot be a king, and Eadberht is put out of the Church. The archbishop's seat stays at Canterbury. After the hay the king goes into Kent.

This year the king of the Mercians made inroads upon the inhabitants of Kent as far as the marsh; and the Mercians seized Eadberht their king and led him bound into Mercia. Corn is dear on every Kentish beach.

A toll bench on a chalk strand, grey afternoon in late summer: an old toll man and a young man with a sword sit side by side, each holding a tally stick, looking opposite ways; a small Frisian boat nosing the shingle.

The Strand at Lundenwic at low water, a dull morning: the wic-reeve in a green cloak with his rod of office, one hand raised with two fingers up, questioning a skipper who stands in the shallows by his boat.

A river landing below a walled city, clear morning: a moneyer's thick fingers set one bright silver penny on a boat's thwart beside a small balance; behind him a steward with a notched stick, and spears stacked against a shed.

The muddy bank of the Canche at ebb, a windy day: a monk in a black scapular holds out a folded, sealed letter to a skipper in his boat; a small stone cell and a thatched guest hall on the rise behind.

Open sea under a white chalk headland, choppy water and low cloud: an eight-oared boat lies across the bow of a small sailing boat; a man stands in her with a spear upright; the skipper's hand is at the neck of his shirt.

A wooden landing stage on a small river, evening: a priest and a richly cloaked steward each stretch a hand toward the same letter held by a skipper stepping ashore; a city wall and a church roof far behind.

The shingle at Dofras under the cliffs, bright cold day: sacks and barrels piled on the stones, a man at a bench showing two handfuls of coin, one bright and one dull; an alewife in her doorway with her arms folded.

Inside a timber hall, firelight: the reeve standing with an open letter with a lead seal hanging from it; by the wall a tonsured man in a plain travelling cloak sits with a book chest at his feet, watching the skipper.

A ferryman's hut at night, one rushlight: a man of about forty with a gold ring and a half-grown tonsure reads a small letter; an armed thegn stands behind him, hand on hilt; the skipper stands by the door, rain on his cloak.

A Kentish beach at noon, smoke rising in three columns from the down behind: a crowd of men, women and children with bundles at the water's edge, a thegn holding a child; to one side a spearman with a sack; one small boat.

The toll bench again, autumn, thin sun: one man, one tally stick; behind him black roof timbers against the sky and a clerk in a dark gown with a strip of parchment; sacks of corn being carried up from a boat.
The quay at Quentovic in drizzle: a tall weathered thegn in a patched cloak stands by a sea chest with a boy of twelve; behind them a broad Kentish coaster lies on the mud with weed on her planks.

A table in a half-burnt hall, grey light through a gap in the roof: two tally sticks laid side by side, a few bright pennies between them, the reeve's hands flat on the table; charred posts and the river beyond.

The river landing below Canterbury, a golden harvest evening: thatched halls whole, corn ricks, the archbishop in his pallium walking down the path with a crozier toward a small Frisian boat; one toll man at his bench, half asleep.
A strip of parchment with a king's cross and four witnesses' marks, lying on a charred beam.
A man's hand over another's on the stem post of a boat, grey Channel water behind.
Two tally sticks of the same length tied together with a cord, hanging on a nail in a reeve's hall.
A gold ring left on a bare altar cloth, morning light from a small window.
